title: Zeno's lost books
hook: Zeno wrote many books, almost all lost; we know him through others (Diogenes Laërtius 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was know again, the old sense of reading, after twelve books read straight through. Your line was read it again.

An ancient biographer copied out a long list of one man's book titles. Not one of those books can be found today. All anyone knows of their author comes from what others said about him, centuries later, some who never met him, some of them rivals. That's the man who started it all. For months this path has read Epictetus, Seneca and Marcus, the Roman Stoics, whose words survived. Now it widens to the school before them, and begins with its founder, whose words almost all vanished.
screen: `A LONG LIST OF TITLES.` → `KNOWN ONLY THROUGH OTHERS.` → `THE FOUNDER'S LOST BOOKS.`

segments.voice: First, who he was. Zeno came from Citium, a town on Cyprus, and made his way to Athens. The story, told by the biographer Diogenes Laërtius, is that he was a merchant who lost his cargo in a shipwreck, and in Athens found philosophy. He studied with the Cynic Crates and others, then taught in a painted colonnade on the edge of the marketplace, the Stoa Poikilē. His followers were called the people of the stoa, the porch: Stoics. Second, the books. Diogenes lists Zeno's titles in book seven of his Lives: a Republic, On Life according to Nature, On the Passions, On What Is Appropriate, On Law, and more. Not one survives whole. What's left are scraps: a sentence quoted here, a summary there, mostly by later writers, some of them critics. Third, what that means. Everything this path has called Stoicism this year comes from people writing centuries after Zeno. The founder is known the way you know a great-great-grandparent: through stories, a few sayings, and family resemblance. And some of his ideas, especially parts of his Republic, were apparently embarrassing to later Stoics, who may have smoothed them over. Fourth, the strange comfort. Zeno's words mostly vanished, and the school was still alive centuries later, when Marcus wrote. What survived wasn't his sentences. It was what his students did with them.
screen: `FROM CITIUM, BY WAY OF A SHIPWRECK.` · `A LIST OF TITLES, NONE SURVIVING.` · `KNOWN THROUGH LATER WRITERS.` · `WHAT LASTED: WHAT STUDENTS DID.` · then, large: `MOSTLY LOST.`

segments.voice: Suppose that a hundred years from now almost nothing you made survives: no files, no photos, only what people remember of how you were. Ask what you'd want carried on, not a sentence or an achievement but a way of being: patient with your kids, honest at work, the friend who showed up. Let one thing come forward, and hold it for a few breaths.
Zeno, the shipwrecked merchant who found philosophy in Athens and taught in a painted colonnade, though almost none of his own books survive. Today's word.
Your line: mostly lost. The part of you worth carrying on doesn't depend on paper. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Students of Stoicism read Zeno through the fragments and reports gathered from later writers, especially Diogenes Laërtius's Lives, book seven.

what it means: Zeno wrote many books, and almost all are lost; we know him through others.
what a scholar hears: Zeno's fragments were gathered by Hans von Arnim in Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta (1903–1905), and ancient reports suggest later Stoics were uneasy with parts of his Republic.

chat.says: If Zeno's books are lost, how does anyone know what the first Stoics taught?
options: Through later writers who quoted and summed him up, some of them critics.
From his own books, found again in a library in Athens.
From Marcus Aurelius, who copied Zeno's books into his notebook.
chat.meaning: Not one of Zeno's books survives whole. What's left are scraps quoted and summarized by later writers, some of them critics.

Citium.meaning: Zeno's hometown, a town on Cyprus

Stoa Poikilē.meaning: the painted colonnade in Athens where Zeno taught

Diogenes Laërtius.meaning: an ancient biographer of the philosophers

Crates.meaning: a Cynic philosopher, one of Zeno's teachers

sources.work: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers

notes: Zeno of Citium c. 334–262 BC; arrival in Athens c. 312 and teaching from c. 300 BC. 'Around 300 BC' is hedged; confirm.
Titles from DL 7.4: Republic, On Life according to Nature, On Impulse or Human Nature, On the Passions, On Duty (the appropriate, kathēkon), On Law, etc. Confirm titles used.
Later Stoics' discomfort with Zeno's Republic: DL 7.32–34 reports critics and some Stoics who called it spurious or early. Hedged; confirm.
'The school lasted five hundred years' (c. 300 BC to the 3rd century AD) is approximate; confirm.
